---
title: "Exact Coordinate Descent for Concomitant Huber Regression"
date: ""
abstract: |
  We implement ROME's exact coordinate descent for sparse Huber regression
  in Python and extend it to joint estimation of regression coefficients
  and scale. The extension preserves the convex Combettes–Müller perspective
  objective: an MM scale step updates both the Huber threshold and the
  coefficient penalty used in the next coordinate sweep. We derive the
  update and its descent property, and handle zero-scale solutions through
  the closed perspective. Experiments compare the original ROME implementation,
  its fixed-scale Python counterpart, and the concomitant extension on the
  original simulation designs. A separate scaling study compares solvers
  for the same unconstrained c-lasso R4 problem. Glass spectra and bacterial
  gene-expression data illustrate cross-validated prediction and a matched
  approximate-message-passing comparison.
---

*Keywords:* concomitant estimation, coordinate descent, Huber regression,
majorization-minimization, perspective function.

# Introduction

Sparse Huber regression combines a quadratic loss for small residuals with
linear growth for large residuals and an $\ell_1$ penalty on the coefficients.
Kim, Loh and Basu [-@kim2025exact] developed exact scalar coordinate updates
for this problem. Their R package ROME combines these updates with screening
and warm starts to compute regularization paths.

The Huber threshold is expressed in response units and therefore depends on
the residual scale. The perspective formulation of Combettes and Müller
[-@combettes2020] estimates scale and coefficients jointly
in a convex problem. Connections between robust loss, sparsity and scale
estimation also appear in @owen2006 and @antoniadis2010. Existing proximal
methods solve the perspective problem, but do not use ROME's exact coordinate
updates.

We implement ROME's fixed-scale coordinate descent in Python, with compiled
numerical routines, and extend it with a scalar majorization–minimization
(MM) update for scale.
The extension changes the threshold, the coefficient penalty, and the
optimality checks after each scale update. It retains the original convex
objective, including its zero-scale boundary. We compare the three
implementations on ROME's simulation designs, then compare algorithms for
identical concomitant objectives and evaluate prediction on two datasets.

# Fixed-scale and concomitant Huber regression

For observations $(y_i,X_i)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^p$, we write
$r_i(\beta)=y_i-X_i^\top\beta$. We display the objectives without an
intercept. When included, the intercept is unpenalized. The Huber loss and its score are
$$
 h_\delta(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 u^2/2,& |u|\le\delta,\\
 \delta|u|-\delta^2/2,& |u|>\delta,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 \psi_\delta(u)=\mathrm{sign}(u)\min\{|u|,\delta\}.
$$
The original ROME objective is
$$
 \widehat\beta_{\delta,\lambda}\in\arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p}
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_\delta(r_i(\beta))
       +\lambda R_\alpha(\beta)\right\},
 \qquad
 R_\alpha(\beta)=\alpha\|\beta\|_1+
                 \frac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-rome}
We focus on the lasso case $\alpha=1$, as in the synthetic experiments
of the ROME paper.

Following the perspective calculus of Combettes and Müller
[-@combettes2018], we define the concomitant estimator by
$$
 (\widehat\beta,\widehat\sigma)\in
 \arg\min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^p,\ \sigma\ge0}
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma),\qquad
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma)=
 \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\widetilde h_\rho(\sigma,r_i(\beta))
 +a\sigma+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1 ,
$$ {#eq-concomitant}
where $\rho,a,\lambda_0>0$ and
$$
 \widetilde h_\rho(\sigma,u)=
 \begin{cases}
 \sigma h_\rho(u/\sigma),&\sigma>0,\\
 \rho|u|,&\sigma=0 .
 \end{cases}
$$
The perspective is jointly convex in $(\sigma,u)$, so
@eq-concomitant is jointly convex in $(\beta,\sigma)$. The constant
$\rho$ is dimensionless. The fitted residual threshold is $\rho\sigma$.
For a standard Gaussian reference, the scale-score calibration is
$$
 a_{\rm G}(\rho)=\tfrac12 E\min\{Z^2,\rho^2\},\qquad Z\sim N(0,1).
$$
The constant $a$ is part of the objective and must be matched between solvers.

At a fixed positive scale, multiplication of the coefficient objective
by $\sigma$ gives
$$
 \arg\min_\beta F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma)
 =
 \arg\min_\beta
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_i h_{\rho\sigma}(r_i(\beta))
          +\sigma\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1\right\}.
$$ {#eq-rescaling}
Thus ROME's scalar update applies with
$\delta=\rho\sigma$ and $\lambda_{\rm inner}=\sigma\lambda_0$.
Both quantities change with scale. $\lambda_0$ remains fixed in the joint
objective.

# Coordinate descent with scale estimation

## The MM scale update

The representation of Huber estimation as least squares with an
$\ell_1$-penalized mean shift appears in @antoniadis2007, @gannaz2006
and @she2011. The sparsity penalty in this
identity acts on observation-specific shifts. It is distinct from the
penalty on regression coefficients. We use it to majorize the scale objective while retaining exact
coefficient updates.

We define $S_\tau(u)=\mathrm{sign}(u)(|u|-\tau)_+$. The mean-shift identity
$$
 \sigma h_\rho(r/\sigma)
 =\min_{o\in\mathbb R}\left\{\frac{(r-o)^2}{2\sigma}+\rho|o|\right\}
$$
has minimizer $o=S_{\rho\sigma}(r)$. For current residuals $r$ and
scale $t>0$, we set $o_i^{(t)}=S_{\rho t}(r_i)$. Holding these values fixed
majorizes the scale objective by
$$
 Q(\sigma\mid t)=
 \frac{\|r-o^{(t)}\|_2^2}{2n\sigma}
 +a\sigma+\frac{\rho}{n}\|o^{(t)}\|_1+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1 .
$$
The majorizer agrees with $F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,t)$ at $\sigma=t$.
Its minimizer is
$$
 \sigma^+=
 \left\{\frac1{2an}\sum_{i=1}^n
                   \min(r_i^2,\rho^2t^2)\right\}^{1/2}.
$$ {#eq-mm-scale}
This is one MM step, rather than an exact minimization of the original
scale block. Algorithm 1 uses $B$ steps before each coefficient sweep. The software
may stop the scale updates earlier at its scale-block tolerance. Numerical
controls and experiment-specific settings are collected in Supplement S1.

## Exact coefficient updates

For coordinate $j$, we define the partial residual $u=r+X_j\beta_j$.
At the current scale, the update solves
$$
 \beta_j^+\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathbb R}
 \left\{\frac1n\sum_i h_\delta(u_i-X_{ij}\theta)+\eta|\theta|\right\},
 \qquad \delta=\rho\sigma,\quad\eta=\sigma\lambda_0 .
$$
Its derivative is affine between the kinks
$u_i/X_{ij}\pm\delta/|X_{ij}|$ for $X_{ij}\ne0$.
The exact root is obtained by sorting these kinks and updating the
cumulative slope, as in ROME. Algorithm 2 gives the scalar subroutine.
Zero design entries contribute neither kinks nor slope.

For stopping, we define $g=-X^\top\psi_\rho(r/\sigma)/n$ and
$$
 \begin{aligned}
 V_j(\beta,g,\lambda_0)&=
 \begin{cases}
 |g_j+\lambda_0\mathrm{sign}(\beta_j)|,&\beta_j\ne0,\\
 (|g_j|-\lambda_0)_+,&\beta_j=0,
 \end{cases}\\
 R_\beta(\beta,r,\sigma,\lambda_0)&=\max_j V_j(\beta,g,\lambda_0),\\
 R_\sigma(r,\sigma)&=
 \left|a-\frac1{2n}\sum_i\psi_\rho(r_i/\sigma)^2\right|.
 \end{aligned}
$$
At positive scale, $R_\beta=R_\sigma=0$ are the joint optimality
conditions. An unpenalized intercept adds the condition $\sum_i\psi_i=0$.

Algorithm 1 follows ROME's pathwise organization
[@kim2025exact, Algorithm 1]. Blue expressions add scale estimation,
rescale the coefficient problem, or replace screening and stopping.
We set $\chi=0$ for fixed scale and $\chi=1$ for concomitant estimation.
We refresh all zero-coordinate checks at the current scale. ROME's
fixed-threshold sequential strong rule is not assumed valid after a scale
change. Coefficients and scale are warm-started along the penalty path,
following the pathwise strategy of @friedman2010.


{{< include algorithm.qmd >}}

## Descent and implementation

Each MM step satisfies
$$
 F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,\sigma^+)
 \le Q(\sigma^+\mid t)\le Q(t\mid t)=F_{\lambda_0}(\beta,t).
$$
Each exact coefficient update also decreases the objective. Thus, at a fixed
penalty, objective values are nonincreasing and converge, since they are
nonnegative. A positive-scale point with $R_\beta=R_\sigma=0$ is a global
minimizer by convexity. This argument establishes descent, rather than a
convergence rate for the coefficient–scale sequence.

The Python implementation retains the breakpoint search and avoids sorting
when a candidate root is verified to remain in its current Huber segment.
It reuses residuals and score evaluations. Both fixed-scale and concomitant
fits can use the same safeguarded support Newton step. Its equations and
settings are given in Supplement S2. A sweep over $m$ coordinates costs
$O(np+mn\log n+Bn)$, including a full optimality check and $B$ scale steps.

Algorithm 1 describes the positive-scale iterations. A zero-scale candidate
requires a separate check: at $\sigma=0$, the objective is LAD-lasso,
$\rho\|y-X\beta\|_1/n+\lambda_0\|\beta\|_1$. The implementation solves
this boundary problem and checks a feasible perspective dual and its
primal–dual gap before declaring joint optimality. Small scale alone is
insufficient. Supplement S3 gives the certificate and the rule for continuing
a path after an approximate return. No positive scale floor is imposed.

# Computational assessment

## ROME simulation designs

We repeat the four designs in Section 4.1 of @kim2025exact. They use
compound Gaussian correlation $0.8$, multivariate $t_2$ with AR($0.8$)
dependence, Gaussian AR($0.8$) predictors with a Cauchy last coordinate,
and Cauchy AR($0.2$) and Gaussian AR($0.8$) blocks. We use the original sparse coefficient vector,
independent $N(0,1)$ response errors, and all nine combinations
$n,p\in\{100,500,1000\}$. Ten replications per setting give 360 datasets.
The original study used 100 replications per setting.

Each implementation receives the same saved data and 100 absolute penalties,
$$
 \Lambda_{\max}=\|X^\top\psi_{0.5}(y)\|_\infty/n,\qquad
 \lambda_\ell=\Lambda_{\max}(0.05)^{\ell/100},\quad \ell=1,\ldots,100.
$$
The endpoint follows the original experimental script. Native R/C ROME fixes
$\delta=0.5$. Python fixed-scale CD uses $\rho=0.5,\sigma=1$.
Concomitant CD uses $\rho=0.5$, $a=a_{\rm G}(0.5)$ and
$\sigma^{(0)}=1$. Both Python modes use the same optimized coefficient
routines and support steps. Their coefficient subproblems coincide initially,
but scale estimation subsequently changes both threshold and penalty.

@fig-rome reports path CPU time with one BLAS thread, excluding
compilation, startup, data loading, serialization and post-fit audits.
Boundary solves and approximate-solution continuation are included. Every
path visits all 100 penalties. Python uses coefficient tolerance
$\epsilon_{\rm sim}$ and limit $K_{\rm sim}$. Concomitant fitting additionally
checks scale optimality or the boundary certificate. Native ROME retains
its own iterate-change tolerance $\epsilon_{\rm ROME}$. These stopping rules
are different, so the native comparison is not accuracy-matched.
The fixed-scale Python curve distinguishes implementation effects from
changes caused by scale estimation.

The fixed-scale and concomitant Python fits certify all penalties on
333/360 and 315/360 paths, respectively. There are 73 and 89 uncertified
points out of 36,000. Their computation remains in the timings and the
corresponding cells are marked. Supplement S3 reports independent objective
bounds and the native-code audit. The curves therefore describe the stated
implementations and numerical returns, rather than a uniform speed guarantee.

![Mean CPU time and standard deviation over ten replications for 100-penalty paths: original R/C ROME, fixed-scale Python CD, and concomitant Python CD. All 360 datasets are included. Hollow Python markers indicate cells containing a path with at least one uncertified return.](../analysis/outputs/optimized-paper/rome-timing.pdf){#fig-rome width=100%}

## Matched concomitant solutions and c-lasso

We next compare algorithms for the same unconstrained objective
@eq-concomitant. In c-lasso 1.0.11 [@simpson2020], R4 uses doubled Huber loss.
Its parameters map to ours as
$$
 \lambda_{\rm classo}=2n\lambda_0,\qquad e=2na.
$$
We use $\rho=1.345$, $a=1/2$, no intercept and no constraints. The audited
comparators are the mean-shift Path-Alg branch and Douglas–Rachford (DR).
We call Path-Alg directly because the R4 path interface otherwise selects
DR. Zero Gram correction preserves the target objective. DR uses metric
parameter $c_{\rm DR}$ and the common accuracy check. Supplement S4 gives
the augmentation, stopping criteria and prepared timing table.

The scaling experiment varies $n$ at $p=2n$ and $p$ at $n=100$, with two
seeds and three timed repetitions. Predictors are standardized independent
Gaussian variables. Ten coefficients are nonzero and errors are Gaussian.
The common penalty is $f_{\rm R4}$ times the maximum score correlation at
the initial MAD scale. A return must satisfy the common coefficient and
scale tolerances $\epsilon_{\rm R4}$ and relative objective tolerance
$\epsilon_{\rm obj}$. Prepared solve times exclude imports, compilation and
model/Gram setup. Setup and total times are recorded separately.

CD and Path-Alg pass these checks in all 30 calls. DR passes in 27.
At $n=200,p=400$, prepared CD takes 5.86 ms, Path-Alg 122.80 ms and
DR 2213.62 ms (@fig-r4). These are implementation timings: CD uses
compiled routines, whereas the c-lasso updates execute at Python level.

![Prepared solve time for the same unconstrained R4 objective. Curves use repetitions passing the common accuracy checks for all methods. Counts and times are given in Supplement S4.](../analysis/outputs/revision-r4/scaling.pdf){#fig-r4 width=100%}

@fig-equivalence shows selected coefficients and scale for a full-rank
$n=80,p=40$ example. The final coefficient differences from Path-Alg are
$4.4\times10^{-8}$ for CD and $2.9\times10^{-7}$ for DR. Scale differences
are $3.9\times10^{-8}$ and $5.8\times10^{-7}$. A CD sweep and a DR update
are different units of work: the iteration axis shows agreement, not speed.

![Three coefficient trajectories, scale, and distance to the Path-Alg solution. Solid curves denote CD, dashed curves denote DR, and horizontal lines give the Path-Alg endpoint.](../analysis/outputs/revision-r4/trajectory.pdf){#fig-equivalence width=100%}

# Real-data applications

## Cross-validated prediction

We use the archaeological glass data from the ROME application
($n=180,p=486$, frequencies 15–500, response PbO) and the *B. subtilis*
riboflavin data ($n=71,p=4088$). Ten random outer splits use training/test
sizes 120/60 for glass and 50/21 for riboflavin. Within each training set,
five-fold CV selects among 50 penalty fractions from 1 to $10^{-3}$.
Each model uses its own intercept-only null-model penalty anchor.
Centering and scaling are fitted within each training fold. For riboflavin,
a deterministic greedy correlation filter retains 500 genes using only
that fold's training predictors. Both models receive the same columns.

Fixed-scale and concomitant fits use the same Python coefficient routines,
an unpenalized intercept, lasso penalties and $\rho=1.345$. The concomitant
constant is $a_{\rm G}(1.345)$. The glass analysis is therefore a lasso
adaptation of the ROME application, which used elastic-net mixing $0.3$.
Uncertified fits are excluded individually from CV, while later penalties
are still attempted. Supplement S5 gives the null anchors, numerical settings
and a representative CV/prediction plot.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/optimized-real/results.qmd >}}

: Held-out MSE divided by the training response variance, and selected coefficient counts. Parentheses give standard deviations over ten outer splits. {#tbl-real}

Prediction errors are similar for the two estimators in these experiments.
Concomitant fitting selects more coefficients on average. All selected
refits pass their accuracy checks. Two concomitant splits exclude one
uncertified penalty from the inner-CV grid. The other grids are complete.
Four of the twenty concomitant refits have certified zero scale.

## A matched riboflavin AMP instance

We also reproduce the specific riboflavin problem in the supplied
Perspective–AMP manuscript [@perspectiveamp], separately from CV prediction.
Its global predictor-only correlation filter retains 500 genes before the
80% training split ($n=57,p=500$). Both algorithms receive this same matrix.
The normalization is
$$
 A=X/\sqrt n,\qquad B=\sqrt n\,\beta,\qquad
 \lambda_{\rm AMP}=\sqrt n\,\lambda_0.
$$
At $\lambda_{\rm AMP}=2.5$ and $\omega=14/500$, both methods select 14
coefficients, with maximum difference $1.6\times10^{-9}$ and fitted scale
$0.55608$. Every timed return passes the common accuracy checks.

{{< include ../analysis/outputs/optimized-paper/amp-matched.qmd >}}

# Discussion

The Python implementation makes ROME's exact fixed-scale coordinate descent
available alongside a concomitant extension. The extension adds a scalar MM
step and updates both $\rho\sigma$ and $\sigma\lambda_0$ before each
coefficient sweep. Current-scale optimality checks and the closed-perspective
boundary are essential to fitting the stated convex objective.

The experiments separate three questions: implementation cost relative to
native ROME, the effect of estimating scale with the same Python routines,
and computation for identical concomitant objectives. Scale updates are
inexpensive, but changing scale can change coefficient sweeps and boundary
costs. Accuracy must therefore accompany runtime. The two prediction studies
illustrate the specified tuning procedures. They do not establish a general
risk advantage. A zero-scale solution is a valid optimum of the closed
objective, rather than an estimate of positive residual noise.

MM is our principal scale update because it gives a simple descent step
using only the residuals. Direct scalar minimization and joint-proximal
splitting remain available in the software. Supplement S6 derives these
alternatives and reports their numerical comparison. The available evidence
does not establish that MM is uniformly fastest.
